utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 16th of July, 2009. I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, first of all, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic, and of course Mr. Coric, the Defence lawyers, Mr. Stewart in particular, Mr. Stringer, as well as his associates, and all the people assisting us. As you know, today is our last day of hearing before our summer recess. We shall resume on the 17th of August. I would like to take the opportunity to wish everyone a well-deserved rest, because when we start again in August, we will have a lot of work ahead of us. We are seeing, actually, the end of the tunnel, since after Mr. Praljak's testimony as a witness, we will hear Mr. Petkovic's, Mr. Coric's and Mr. Pusic's witnesses. So this is now the final part of these proceedings. As I have said, everyone should get a good rest to prepare for the time when we resume. I know that some of the accused will be able to go home and have a rest at home. Others, for specific reasons, cannot benefit from this. As you know, pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure, some have been granted a provisional release; others have not. This has been ruled by the Appeals Chamber. The Bench sitting in front of you was in favour of enabling some of the accused of contacting their relatives during the summer recess. I therefore would like to wish all and everyone, as I've just said, a well-deserved rest so that we resume in the best conditions possible in August. As you know, all of this is extremely taxing, and we need to have breaks from time to time. From what I understood, Mr. Stewart wanted to take the floor, if he so wishes. Now's the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Just very briefly, Your Honours. And I'm not sure what I've done to deserve a specific welcome this morning, but thank you. That's appreciated, of course. Your Honours, I'm speaking for myself and Mr. Khan on this point. We have seen Your Honours' orders, of course, and Your Honours' order yesterday in relation to the questions that have been referred now to the disciplinary council of the ADC, and Mr. Khan and I are both members of that council. But I just wanted to reassure Your Honours and everybody else concerned that actually some days before the order, we had seen straightaway that we should not participate, so we have had absolutely no participation in any discussion of the merits of the matter, and nor will we do. So, in effect, we've -- well, I suppose it's not a bad thing. We've complied with Your Honours' order in advance, which can never be a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. As all's been said, I shall give the floor back to Mr. Stringer, who will resume his cross-examination on the basis of the third binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm assuming that you still have in front of you the Presidential transcript we were talking about yesterday at the end, P00089. And when we ended the day yesterday, we were on page 17, and we were -- we were -- I can put it this way: We were debating the meaning of some of the phrases and words that are in there. And I was thinking last night about how to get through this without opening up the Pandora's Box again of this issue of "podrucje" versus "territory," because I think that it's something that's been pretty fully fleshed out in terms of the views --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly repeat your sentence, Mr. Stringer. One word is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I've been asked to repeat what I'm saying. I was thinking last night about how to talk about this issue without opening up again the Pandora's Box of this issue of "podrucje" versus "territory." And, General, you've heard a lot of testimony and statements about that issue. Zoran Buntic is one of the witnesses whom I think we talked about that a lot. And I'm going to try and get at this from a different angle to avoid argument or debate about what "podrucje" is and what "territory" is, and so let's see if we can get at this from another perspective. And, actually, I'm going to start by hopefully using a word that we can both work with, accepting that we agree to disagree, perhaps, in terms of ultimately what the objectives were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I'm allowed an observation, the word in the original text here is not "podrucje," it is "prostorno," so just for the record that there doesn't arise later on the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes. I do recognise that. It seemed to me that we were starting to go back down that road anyway yesterday, and so it seemed to me that perhaps something that's a little more neutral that we can work with, while we agree to disagree, is the English word "space," which is actually the word in the French translation that came through, "espace."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, so I'm going to suggest to you that that's perhaps a word that I can use that we can work with in a way to avoid a more difficult debate about territory. So yesterday, when we finished off, we were looking at this one paragraph, this statement of Mate Boban, where he's talking about certain events or contingencies which if they were to take place, could result in the proclamation of independent Croatian territory. And the first question I have for you, General, is this: Without getting into a debate about what could have triggered such a proclamation, what conditions could have given rise to that, if you'll just bear with me and assume that whatever those conditions were, they did come to pass, had there been a proclamation of independent Croatian territory, as Boban refers to here, do you know what the territory or the space would have consisted of? Would it have been actually the territory or the space of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, not at all, for the simple reason that Croatia, Herceg-Bosna -- Croatian Herceg-Bosna was composed of an entire series of -- how should I put it? I can talk about Croatian terms and their meaning in a certain context, but wherever there were a few Croats in Central Bosnia around Usora and so on and so forth, they became a political entity within Herceg Bosnia, with an organisation that was first and foremost involved in defence, because -- yes, that's not possible, that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then it seems to me, General, that this concept of accession is something that really is inconsistent with your interpretation of Boban's words. If you're talking about little pockets of Croat people scattered throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, the fact is that there's no way that such pockets could accede to the Croatian state; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's -- if this includes the assumption that you've made, and it's all a matter of making assumptions, well, in such an event, such pockets, and we're talking about your assumption, not about the reality when we're talking about acceding to the Croatian state, so even if such a state had come to pass, even if there was such a reality, such pockets couldn't have acceded to Croatia. And I'm saying "if." But I'll repeat what I have said. Without the international community, this is something that would not have been possible or that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, here Mate Boban continues, and he says that if there is an accession, that this would happen only "at such a time as the Croatian leadership, in whom our people until now have placed their complete trust, should decide that the moment and the time has come." Now, you've talked about the fact that in the Croatian Constitution, it made President Tudjman, in fact, the president of all the Croatian people, no matter where they're located, and what's happening here, then, in making this statement, is that Boban's acknowledging, isn't he, that, in fact, President Tudjman is his president, and it's President Tudjman whose policies and decisions will be those that will guide and govern Boban and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. In the Croatian Constitution, it doesn't say that President Tudjman is the president of all the Croats, as far as I know. That's not possible. The HDZ party, which was founded in various parts of the world, said that President Tudjman was also their president in the creation of the Croatian state, that this problem is one that can't be understood if one doesn't regard the situation Croatia was in at the time, or, rather, if one doesn't regard the situation the entire Yugoslavia was in at the time, together with the entire international community that would change its policies towards Yugoslavia from month to month, not to say from day to day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 19 of this text. And here Ignjac Kostroman begins talking, and what he does -- we'll skip over, I'm not going to read it all, but what he does is to read the minutes of a meeting that was held on the 23rd of December, 1991, which is just four days before this meeting, and he's reading out the minutes of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in an expanded session with members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ party. And first of all, General Praljak, you know Ignjac Kostroman. Here he's acting as secretary, I believe -- yes, secretary of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and administrative secretary of the Croatian Democratic Union. You knew Ignjac Kostroman. I think about a year after this, in December of 1992, you were present with him at that rally in Zenica, weren't you, where you showed us the footage when you were talking to the soldiers about not smoking?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet him, but I didn't really know him. We met briefly, perhaps on two or three occasions at the most, but I don't think it was even three occasions during that entire period. So I did meet him, but I did not really know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in item 2 on page 21, Kostroman is reading from the minutes of this meeting of the Presidency of the HZ-HB, and they're informing President Tudjman of these conclusions. And item 2 says that: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has once again confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on 18 November 1991 in Grude, taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." Now, again, without getting into the debate about what the word "territories," or "space," or whatever it is means there, the fact is, isn't it, General, that what the HZ-HB people wanted, at least those who are signing off on these minutes, is the delineation of a Croatian space in Bosnia-Herzegovina which then would serve as the basis for accession to the Republic of Croatia; isn't that what this is about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says that it represents a legal basis, a legal basis, a possibility. It's put conditionally, since the Serbs had already broken up Bosnia and Herzegovina and no one knew what was to come. So this was a time at which various possibilities were being examined, and that's all. So if such and such thing occurs, then such and such a thing will follow, and so on and so forth. It was a normal political discussion on the subject of the fate of the people, and no one knew what their fate would be because the Serbs had all the key elements in their hands with their aggression, and there was also the international community that was adapting to that situation. So these actors were in control of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, he hasn't spoken yet, I don't believe, but Stjepan Kljujic, who actually at this time is the president of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina, he's present at this meeting. Item 8 on page 23 makes a direct reference to him. This is again item 8 that Kostroman is reading from the minutes, expressing the disapproval or criticism of Stjepan Kljujic. It says: "Kljujic, president of the HDZ, does not have the legitimacy of the HDZ organs to act independently as a representative at state and inter-party negotiations crucial to the interests of Croats in this territory, so he is hereby once again denied that right." So we're going to talk about this more, General, but what's happening here at this meeting is the beginning of the end of Stjepan Kljujic and the beginning of the beginning for Mate Boban and people who shared his views, as opposed to the views of Kljujic. Would you agree with me that Kljujic was on his way out as of this time because he did not enjoy the support of those acting as the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Kljujic was a member -- well, no, that's not how I would put it. Stjepan Kljujic isn't being completely limited. He's just said that he can't act independently, so obviously according to this document and the information that I obtained, Stjepan Kljujic started pursuing his own policies as if they were party policies, and naturally people, as is the case in any party, protested and said that in such public discussions, appearances, and negotiations that are of crucial importance for the Croats, it's necessary to consult the people whose fate is being decided. Obviously, Stjepan Kljujic didn't proceed in this way, so they denied him the right to act independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, again, we'll get to this. And so what happened after this meeting, or in the weeks that followed, is that Kljujic resigned or left, he was followed for a brief period of time by Mr. Brkic, and then ultimately he was replaced by Mate Boban, who not only was the president of Herceg-Bosna, but he was also the president of the HDZ party in BH. Would you agree with me on that sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a large extent, but Mate Boban didn't take up Kljujic's position, and Kljujic also took up the position of the previous president of the HDZ. So it was politically normal. The party elects its own president in a democratic manner, and I don't see why this should be the subject of dispute, especially in legal proceedings. Kljujic also replaced the former president of the party, and nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on page 29 of this transcript, we see President Tudjman talking. Actually, on page 27, you'll see he begins and he says: "All right, gentlemen. I was unaware of these conclusions, but I did know that there were differences among you, too, with respect to the strategy of the Croatian policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Would you agree with me, General, that what he's alluding to here are differences between the Boban people, on the one hand, and the Kljujic people, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the discrepancies were far greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on page 29, President Tudjman is talking, and he says: "In addition, if Bosnia and Herzegovina was to remain whole, what are Croatia's prospects there? Gentlemen, when Croatia acceded to the joint Yugoslav state, Croatians made up 24 per cent of the population. Today, they account for a mere 17 per cent. It is quite certain that now that a sovereign, independent Croatian state has been established, the Croatian man will continue to emigrate, as he has done before, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, they will now rush to Croatia in even greater numbers, so that those Croatian areas will be left with ever-decreasing populations and significant Croatian features will increasingly disappear from the area." I'm going to continue on. And what he's talking about here, by the way, at the very beginning is what happens if Bosnia and Herzegovina were to remain whole; right? He continues, page 30: "Under the present circumstances, gentlemen, from the general Croatian standpoint, a demarcation of borders suits us better from the general Croatian standpoint and from the standpoint of the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is not the first time that we have talked like this, even in this circle. For tactical reasons we did not raise, because we did not want to be the ones to raise it, the issue of borders, but in the draft Hague Conference on Yugoslavia and generally in the world, which suits us, and the position is even reiterated by the United States, even in the letter I received today from the State Department, it says that they oppose any changing of borders by force. However, it seems to me that conditions are becoming ripe for a political agreement on demarcation in Bosnia-Herzegovina because the world is opposed to war. It would begin because either the army in Bosnia or the Serbs would start it. Certainly, we are not going to start it, just as we did not start it in Croatia." So at this point, the fact -- well, let me just continue, and then we'll come back. Moving across to page 31: "In other words, the survival, the sovereignty of Bosnia in the present circumstances from the Croatian standpoint is such that not only do we not have to advocate it, we must not even raise the issue openly. However, why not accept this offer of demarcation when it is in the interests of the Croatian people, the Croatian people here in this republic and the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I do not see a single reason -- a single serious reason against it. Moreover, in the talks that I personally conducted with Izetbegovic and Milosevic, in addition one of our people in Bosnia drafted a proposal for demarcation whereby the Croatian areas and those that you have included in this Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Community of Croatian Posavina, in the event of demarcation, Croatia would get not only those two communities, but also, for geopolitical reasons, Cazinska and Bihac Krajina, which would satisfy almost ideally the Croatian national interests, not only present but also for the future, and then from the remaining areas where ..." And he continues on. Now, General, when President Tudjman here talks about demarcation of borders as "suiting us better from the Croatian standpoint," can we agree that he's correct on that? I mean, Croatia's shape, we know that President Tudjman considered it to be an abnormal shape. We know he considered its borders to be absurd. That was the word he used in one of the other things -- other documents we looked at. So the fact is that he's right when he says that a demarcation of borders is -- would be favourable for Croatia, it would be in Croatia's interest to achieve some change in the borders, even if by political agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have read or what you have read out is the wisdom of a politician. He speaks about what America and other parts of the world will offer. It's an offer for demarcation. If such an offer is made, he says that the Croats won't go to war, won't start a war. He says that the world is against war, and that is why demarcation might occur. And if that were the case, if such an offer were made, there's no reason for Croatia not to accept such demarcation. People create states. It's not the other way around. France did not first come into existence and then the French people -- the French people were there first and then they created their state. That was also the case for the Americans. They rebelled against the English, and they created a state they could live in, a state in which they could arrange their affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And such a state with different borders, borders that would encompass these areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and Posavina that he refers to here on page 31, those borders would, in fact, have been very beneficial for Croatia to achieve; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Croatia became part of the first and the second Yugoslavia, a very significant Croatian population lived there, actually an absolute majority, and so there would be no reason against the Croats living in a single state, should that be offered by someone as a resolution of the Yugoslav or Bosnian-Herzegovinian crisis which ended with the Srebrenica incident. So Mr. Tudjman is here speaking, If this happens, then that can happen, et cetera. So there was a political situation in which nobody had a clue as to what was -- what the international community was up to, but we knew what the Serbs were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, turn to page 34, General, and I'm going to ask you -- I'm going to come back to a passage here that Judge Antonetti asked you about on the 15th of June, although he didn't refer -- at the time he asked you about this, he was referring to paragraph 24 of the pre-trial brief, and he indicated that it would be useful to know the precise location of this quote that he found in the pre-trial brief. Top of page 34, this is Tudjman talking: "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders. "Whether that would be exactly 30 municipalities or 28, even from that viewpoint, that is less important." Now, again, what is happening here, General, isn't it, is that President Tudjman is telling the contingent of the HDZ from Herceg-Bosna, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, he's telling the Herceg-Bosna representatives here what policy is or should be, which is to extend Croatia's borders to the widest extent possible to include as many Croatian people possible inside those borders? Now, of course, we're talking about extending those borders into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that what the Croatian policy is becoming at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They are merely considering options there. If there is a historical moment, and it so happened that after 800 years of the Croatian -- a Croatian state was finally established because up to that time Croatia had always been ruled by powerful imperial forces and other forces, so if, in accordance with international rules, an offer should be made, it can be accepted, there is no reason why it shouldn't be accepted, to avert the war. And here he's saying that it isn't essential how many municipalities should be there. So whether all the municipalities that were parts of the HZ-HB are fewer, that's what President Tudjman says, but this was one of the options on the table after Croatia had been recognised by about a dozen countries, and the Serbs are still controlling a third of Croatian territory. And there were talks in Split. All the presidents had had about 40 talks so far, and everything depended on the international community. So President Tudjman also goes on to say that this was a very delicate issue, and this is how a statesman should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He uses a word here which I think is less controversial than "territory," "podrucje" or another word. He uses the word "opcina," which is given to us in English as "municipality." Now, the fact is that what he envisioned as being beneficial to the interests of Croatia is the borders being extended to include municipalities, not parts of municipalities, or space, or pockets where Croats lived, but, in fact, a group of 30, or 28, or some defined number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And isn't it true, General, that really that's the only way that such a change could be workable or even realistic? Whole municipalities, a well-defined area with borders, is the only way that this beneficial change could be implemented if it were to become available?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't stated this way anywhere. This is a speech about municipalities. The president isn't dealing with petty things here. I completely disagree with your statement, because from this little speech in this transcript, you are drawing conclusions that are false and they are not logically connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Boban then says that: "The founding municipalities of the HZ-HB now have a population which, according to the census, is 55 per cent Croatian, 27 per cent Muslim, 9 per cent Serbian, and the rest are none of the above. "However, because municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were created similarly as in Croatia, by composing Serbian and Muslim population in the territory of Croatia or vice versa, by cleansing border areas, practically border areas of Herceg-Bosna, this creates approximately 65 per cent of the Croatian population in Herceg-Bosna." And he says: "And, pardon me, according to what I know, the most recent data from Serbia are 63 per cent." So, now what Boban's saying here is that in order to achieve this Croatian space, they could enhance that space by clearing out Muslims or non-Croats from certain border areas within HZ-HB and thereby ensure for themselves a clear majority in the territory of the HZ-HB; isn't that what he's saying? It's going to be necessary to move some people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that isn't correct here. What this is about is the following: Exactly due to the wish -- due to the desire for domination in the 1980s, the municipalities were reorganised. I believe that this was conducted by Hamdija Pozderac. But this is not cleansing, it's not cleansing, it's something different altogether. The way municipalities were established was that either a Serbian or a Muslim majority should be in existence everywhere, and by reorganisation, this can be achieved, but there is no -- there is no talk about cleansing. Why, then, not cleanse everybody out of the area, and why have 27 per cent of Muslims? That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, he's talking about a way to increase the Croat population from 55 per cent to 65 per cent within the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By restructuring the municipalities, parts of municipalities that subsequently were added to those municipalities to achieve political effects in Yugoslavia, so by the restructuring of municipalities the same number of Croats would merely constitute a larger share, a higher percentage; no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: President Tudjman continues and says: "It seems to me, therefore, that with a prudent policy, a clever demarcation and agreement with the Serbs in Bosnia, we can even achieve that instead of war, which is threatening because of this unresolved issue and the army build-up, that the army will serve as a guarantee for implementation of such a demarcation." So this brings us back, doesn't it, General, to the issue of Karadjordjevo and the testimony that we read of President Mesic, when he was here on that subject, the article written by Muhamed Filipovic, that in fact an agreement with the Serbs could be achieved whereby a demarcation suiting the interests of Croatia could take place? I mean, Tudjman believed this was possible, clearly, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the opposite of what you're saying is true. Seven or eight months before this, had he struck an agreement with Milosevic in Karadjordjevo about the carve-up, he wouldn't be saying this. He is asking for a sovereign Bosnia. So the last sentence is: "Actively negotiate both with Karadzic and Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman is trying to understand the overall international and Serb policy, trying to find some conditional solutions to avoid war, people dying, and also satisfying the minimum Croatian interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If there had been an agreement with Milosevic, this conversation wouldn't have taken place. There would have been a division of Bosnia between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I have to correct the transcript. Page 18, line 12, President Tudjman said "actively negotiate both with Karadzic and Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I said, that's why it is impossible to take out small portions of such a complex -- from such a complex text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The interpreters were struggling to keep up with you, so I understand -- Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I first thought nothing would come of it, but I think it has worked in the end. Mr. Praljak, I would like to come back to the speech of Mr. Boban, where, in the English translation, he speaks of cleansing border areas. I don't know whether you can identify the passage in the original text. If so, I would be grateful if you could read it out so that we can hear whether "cleansing" is, in fact, a correct translation. It must be on page 35, in the top -- in the top paragraph. "Ciscenjem," is that the word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, but let me read out the whole sentence, because the whole sentence matters. I quote: "However, as the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are something similar to those in Croatia, they were created to or by composing Serbian and Muslim population in the space of Croatia, or vice versa, by cleansing border areas, practically or in fact border areas of Herceg-Bosna [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnia-Herzegovina"]. This creates approximately 65 per cent of Croatian population in this same Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I only was eager to have clarification that the translation is correct, and that has now been established. Excuse me, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Just for the record, page 19, line 18 says "Bosnia-Herzegovina," and I think that it should read "Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the municipalities were created in such a manner. But, yes, without the initial part of the sentence, the municipalities were created in such a way as to get a majority of Serbs in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is not how this sentence of Mate Boban can be understood or interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: Having in mind this question by Judge Trechsel, and there is wording by Mr. Kljujic, who is already mentioned here, on page 111. That is why -- I'm quoting: "That is why we said that we should have commission for cantonisation. Furthermore, inside Bosnia and Herzegovina, we should redraw several municipalities which the parties have set up to our detriment. We should transfer Dobratici to Travnik or Jajce, where it used to be. Other areas, Ravno, for example, should be transferred to Neum," and so on. So that's talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, your intervention, is it a question, or a point of clarification, or is it an argument that you're putting forward?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: I understood that Judge Trechsel asked the meaning of word "ciscenje," and this is the explanation about that. This is at least my understanding. Maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prlic, I think that is not a proper intervention. You have been granted the right to ask questions, but now you are practically arguing, like a lawyer, and even the lawyers at this point are not supposed to argue. I asked the question about the language, and that was given, and nothing else was raised by me. I did not approach the merits. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me if I misunderstood that. I just tried to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do excuse you, of course. I mean, you are not a lawyer, and we're learning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if you would turn to page 39, please. I want to spend some time on some passages that perhaps we haven't focused on previously in the trial. On page 39, a man named Barac is speaking. Do you know who Neven Barac is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you look on page 38, you'll see that he introduces himself as -- he says: "I will say a few words about the work of the Croatian Democratic Union deputies in the Parliament in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am the president of the caucus." And you'll see at the bottom of page 38, he says: "We have advocated this for the following reasons. We believe that such a Bosnia, if it were to stay integral, would benefit most of Croatia and the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then on page 39, he says: "I wanted to say this only so we could hear a position now on how to act from here on in. "We have had this position so far for these reasons and, secondly, because the Muslims have matured and created a nation, whether we admit it or not. They do not accept the ideas of dividing the Bosnia of 60 years ago. "How we will ever win over these 38 municipalities, that is, the municipalities with Muslim population, I do not know. "It is not a question at all of Western Herzegovina, where Croats are 98.8 per cent of the population in Grude. That is not a question at all. It is a question of the other part where we are mixed. That is why I have described how we have worked so far." And moving across to page 41, Boban intervenes or speaks and says: "I think the Muslim people are practically -- I'm not defending them, when it comes to my personal opinion. I would also want Croatia, the one in the borders of 50, 60 years ago, but I think that is hard to divide them. They are a people with their own firm positions, and I think that it will be very hard. As soon as Herceg-Bosna emerged, there were objections from Jablanica, for instance, and from other places, which are not accepting such conceptions. "We may confront each other in some way, and that will, it seems to me, subside." Now, what's happening here is that you have a voice, this person named Barac, who's saying that this Herceg-Bosna concept or a banovina-type concept from 60 years ago, 60 years prior, simply wouldn't work or it couldn't work in anything other than the most highly Croatian areas in Western Herzegovina. The problem he raises is that the people are mixed throughout these territories, throughout much of these territories; isn't that true? There are always going to be difficulties because of the extent to which Croats and Muslims were mixed in many of the areas of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Barac is the vice-president of the caucus of the HDZ, as I see, and they advocate a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina in its existing borders. And this text -- this entire text speaks about a democratic discussion within a party and a very delicate situation, as President Tudjman put it. And Mate Boban said exactly what he said; that the Muslims are a corpus with firm positions, a body with firm positions. And here the people are speaking about options, but these options are always conditional. If the Muslims should agree with the Serbs to join Yugoslavia, what should be done then, and what should be done if not, and -- but there is always the distinction between an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, which refers to its borders, and a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, as interpreted by the Muslims, is a unitary state. And we will see later that the Croats cannot agree to such a unitary state because equality is always insisted upon. And I hope that you will arrive at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can assure you, we'll arrive at that, though it might be after the summer recess. General, Boban here says that what he wants, actually: "What I would also want Croatia, the one in the borders of 50, 60 years ago." Now, we can talk about under what conditions that might take place, but the fact is, and it seems fairly evident, that Boban, as well as Tudjman, would like to have had a Croatia that extended back to the area of the banovina from 1939, which is, of course, what they're referring to here when they say "50 to 60 years ago"; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, if it had been possible to avoid a war or -- and if that could be achieved by agreement with the two other peoples, I can tell you right here I would prefer to be part of a Croatian state than a Bosnia-Herzegovinian state. That's my political right. Why should anybody be guilty of that? Why wage war for that? Franjo Tudjman said, We won't wage war for that. But if it should be agreed with everybody, and if it should become legally possible, why not? And that's the entire story. I mean, why beat about the bush?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I take your point, General, but it seems to me that what Boban here does is actually he anticipates the opposite. He anticipates that it's going to be something that won't be achievable by peaceful means. He's anticipating that, in fact, there may be a confrontation with the Muslims. "We may confront each other." Quite prophetically, he anticipated the possibility of conflict on this issue, and he says: "It seems to me that this will subside." So here in December of 1991, General, let me put it to you this way: Boban's identified what it is he'd like to see happen. He anticipates that there's going to be confrontation with the Muslims that results from that, and he underestimates the extent to which the Muslims will agree to the vision of Herceg-Bosna that he -- that he advocates; isn't that true? All of you underestimated the extent to which the Muslims or the armija in Bosnia and Herzegovina would resist the policies and the aspirations, once it came time for implementation, that are being expressed here in this conversation between Boban and Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite wrong, Mr. Stringer. Boban says, We can do this. Perhaps there will be a conflict, but things will calm down. That's the first thing. And, secondly, Alija Izetbegovic had already written his Islamic Declaration, Mr. Stringer. And two or three months after this, the Croats voted in a referendum and allowed Badinter's commission to say, Yes, we can legally found this state on international terms. After these discussions, three months later these very same Croats held a referendum and confirmed the international legal status of a whole Bosnia and Herzegovina -- of an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina. If anything of what you had said were correct, we would never have held a referendum. We would have reached an agreement with the Serbs, and things would have looked completely different. Your theses are not correct and they have no basis in reality. And up until the -- well, the conflict with the ABiH occurred much later because they weren't prepared, and the Serbs took 70 per cent of the territory. They should have reacted then. They should have prevented ABiH attacks on Croatia at the time, and so on and so forth, everything that you have said. But they failed to do that, so they tried to make up for a lack of territory by acting to the detriment of the Croats. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, we're going to talk about this at length later on, but the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO, in fact, was about their resistance to this implementation of Herceg-Bosna that was going to be taking place in the months following this very conversation. Isn't that essentially what the conflict was about, competing views of what this area of Herceg-Bosna should look like inside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct either. Look, this is in 1991, and the ABiH and the conflict between -- well, it wasn't a conflict between the ABiH and the HVO, it was the aggression of the ABiH on Konjic, Travnik and so on, against Croats, and this was contrary to the internationally-signed agreements on what Bosnia and Herzegovina should look like. Well, please, allow me to complete my sentence. You can't interrupt me all the time. I have the right to complete at least one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm going to continue putting the Prosecution case to you, and if you don't accept it, you can say so, and you do that. But at the same time, you know how it works with time, and every time I put the Prosecution case to you can't be an invitation for you to take a lot of time making a speech. You've said all of these things before. You've given very lengthy testimony, and I think you've really been given every opportunity to express your own views. So I think we need to try to find a balance here between -- I'm trying to give you the space to answer the questions without taking up too much time. General, could you please pass over to page 74, then, of this transcript and this continuing debate, conversation, that's taking place with President Tudjman in Zagreb. At this point, on page 74, Dario Kordic speaks up, introduces himself as the president of the Busovaca HDZ Municipal Board, chair of the Travnik Regional Community, vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And then on page 75, he says: "I think that the Croatian spirit in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Posavina, and particularly in Bosnia, has grown stronger during the past 40 days since the Croatian Community was declared in Grude than it had in the entire year since the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina. "The Croatian people in the region, subregion of Travnik, live with the idea of acceding to the Croatian state, and they are ready to do so at all costs. The young men are teeming with the Croatian spirit. "I say this because I come from the field. We have visited every single village in the territory of this subregional community of Herceg-Bosna." The next paragraph, he's talking about the many Croatian flags on the houses, and the municipalities on the Bosnian part. Continuing over to the next page, he says: "I think that any other option would be considered treason, save the clear demarcation of Croatian soil in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, and preservation against destruction of the Croatian body politic through a well-defined state mechanism of the Croatian state serving as a guarantor to the Croats of Herceg-Bosna, even if only for three months or a year. However, we must believe in it." Now, General, we can -- we can talk about differing views, and we're going to continue to talk about differing views here, but here now we have the vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna talking in no -- talking very clearly and unequivocally about at least his own view that, in fact, accession to the Croatian state is the goal; isn't that true? Wasn't that the goal of at least some of the people who were in the leadership positions of the HDZ in BH and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, as you have said, that there were people who had this objective, and they would express themselves in fierce political 15 terms to encourage themselves. He was in such an awkward position. But at the end of page 76, you have the reasons for which he expresses himself in such perhaps extreme terms. Dario Kordic had read the Islamic Declaration. He mentions the 71 per cent of Muslims that are mentioned there. He says that the Muslims want a civil republic, and I've told you about the text where I said Alija Izetbegovic said either a civil republic or a civil war. At the time, there was Cengic's statement that their house was in Turkey and that there was applause by the SDA party for Libyan and other Islamic ambassadors. They said that these people, this world, was heading towards religious unification and not towards the creation of a modern state of equal people. So Dario Kordic was upset by this, and that's why he said what he said. That's his right, to express his political opinion. But later he has to go to a referendum about Bosnia and Herzegovina. Later, he was overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you'll skip over to page 84 for another of the voices from the competing camp or the competing point of view, if I can put it that way. This is Ivan Markesic. He introduces himself as secretary-general of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Page 85, he says: "When I learned of the forming of the Community of Herceg-Bosna and Croatian Posavina, I thought, and thus tried to fit it into HDZ positions, that it represented a special form of expression of the political will of people living in a certain area. However, in Duvno I became convinced that it is a territorial organisation, while everything in the decision on founding is quite a different matter. I would like to say that the positions expressed here show a clear split in the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the party in which I am the general secretary. I could not and, I must confess, I still cannot reconcile myself to this manner of forming communities for a simple reason. How can I -- with what morality can I receive the Croats from Banja Luka, the 29.000 from Zenica, where there are more than 20.000, or 20.000 from Tuzla, over 34.000 from Sarajevo?" And he asks: "What about an integral solution for the Croatian question in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I estimate that in certain areas where there are compact Croatian entities, there is an aspiration. After all, who of us would not like to live in the state of Croatia? I take this opportunity to salute its recognition. However, I think that the real circumstances in which we find ourselves will not permit this. The circumstances in which Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina live, the people they meet, the political options, none of this will allow it. I do not know how it would be possible in Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf or Travnik, just to say suddenly, We are going into Herceg-Bosna and we will be joined to the Republic of Croatia. "We can wish for this, but I must tell you openly you live here in Zagreb and probably I can tell you sincerely you can have quite a different view of our area down there. We who live down there who all the time are meeting those people who are tied to that piece of land that we live on, where we are a constitutive part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You see these things quite differently, thinking it is simple and convenient to join all of this up, saying, in the name of the Croatian people, that you would join it all to Croatia." And he goes on, and he points out another problem with the policy, or the plan, or the aspiration that's being discussed by others at this meeting. He says, quote, on page 89: "Excuse me, but we are also starting with the facts. Forgive me for saying so, but in this way, with this partition, you are making possible for the first time for Serbia to expand into the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it has never been before." So, now, this is a dissenting voice, this is a different opinion, General, and it's the opinion of someone who's not from Herzegovina; isn't that true? This is the opinion of a Croat, secretary-general of the HDZ party, who comes from an area where Croats are mixed, where they lived with Muslims, where they lived with others, and he's very clearly of the view that the partition that he believes is being discussed here is simply not achievable; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, he expresses that view, but you can see what his position is, and that his opinion is partially different. Mention is made of Franjo Tudjman's position, too, that dates back to 1989, his position on an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, but a solution to the Croatian issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the solution to the Croatian problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at that point in time such a solution was between the Serbian option -- somewhere to be found between the Serbian option of taking 70 per cent of the territory and the Muslim Islamic Declaration. And Markesic, at the end, says the HDZ should persist with its request for a sovereign BH for as long as it's possible for this to be attained, but if this is not possible, in such a situation we'll opt for a different solution. So, Mr. Stringer, it's an open, broad discussion that involves people who are democratically looking for a solution. There is no solution mentioned here. Only possibilities are mentioned. And the meeting referred to in Tomislavgrad, as far as I heard, didn't bear any fruit, no conclusions were adopted or published in HDZ documents, and therefore the people were desperate. I mean, well, they had no idea about what was going to happen, apart from the fact that they thought that someone was going to -- or was preparing to kill them, as was the case in Vukovar, Dubrovnik, and so on and so forth. And, furthermore, add to that the embargo and see how you would manage in such a situation. You're waiting to be slaughtered like cattle under such an embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Page 90, Ignjac Kostroman begins talking. We can skip over that. He says: "Many harsh words have just been said against Herceg-Bosna, as if it were a case of a classic conspiracy against the sovereignty of BH." And then he goes on. He's critical of Stjepan Kljujic, which we can move over. I want to go now to page 98. President Tudjman starts speaking.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, which page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 98. It would be good to read out when Kostroman says this isn't a conspiracy against the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is a discussion. But, well, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, no one denies this is a discussion, General. It's a discussion, would you agree with me, that sheds light on differing views and visions for the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't that what this is about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The subject is how to survive without war, how to adopt the international -- adapt to the international community, how to reach an agreement with the other two peoples, how to save lives, how to find out what the international community wants, in fact, and how to avoid errors and lose everything, which is what the situation was for 800 years because that's how the policies of the great powers pursued, and so on and so forth. So that's the problem. Your country, Mr. Stringer, is powerful. We were just wondering what to do in order to ensure our survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And one of the threats to the survival of the Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna, I think it's not controversial, is the fact, and President Tudjman alludes to it earlier in the same discussion, the fact that the numbers of Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina are diminishing and have been trending downward for a number of years, particularly after the establishment of the Croatian state. I mean, it was a well-known and recognised fact that the percentage of the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina was declining; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman mentioned something that's called a sociological law. If you create a poor state for people, then the people from that state disappears. Yugoslavia was bad for the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, you're not answering my question. Is it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very well. I don't understand your question. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, earlier here in this transcript we saw President Tudjman state that the percentage of the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina had declined from 25 per cent, I believe it was, to 17 per cent. Do you recall that? And that was the truth, isn't it? That was a concern?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The percentage was even greater before. There was the imperial conquering of Karadjordjevic's Yugoslavia. There was domination, the relationships hadn't been arranged, and as a result the number of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina diminished, as well as in Croatia. So now throughout the world, there are more than three and a half million of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On page 98 of the transcript, President Tudjman begins speaking, and he says: "All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people." And he goes on talking about the creation of Bosnia as part of colonial conquests of an Asian power, at the expense of the Croatian people and Croatian territories, between the 15th and 18th centuries. So this is a reference, isn't it, to the Ottoman Empire? And then he goes on to talk about the Communist -- continue on to page 99. After recounting this history, he says: "Therefore, Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something God given which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is. "Because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory. Regarding administration, not to mention defence, we cannot establish an independent Croatia such as it is." Now, General, the fact is that if Tudjman's not satisfied with an independent Croatia, such as it is, on the 27th of December, 1991, then what he's looking to do is to extend the borders of Croatia, to redraw borders, and to push the border eastward into Bosnia-Herzegovina, with ultimately restoration of the banovina as being the ultimate goal or most desirable objective; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. President Tudjman spoke about historical circumstances, and, Mr. Stringer, historical circumstances were such that we served only as a base. They would take children and turn them into Turkish soldiers. They did that for several centuries. They would take children from us. So your thesis is not correct. Tudjman was a rational politician. He has the right to historical reflection, and he wrote an excellent book that is called "Big Ideas and Small Peoples." When you have big ideas, small peoples disappear. Yes, I've answered your question. Your thesis is not correct. I completely disagree with it. He examined the possibility that the Serbs -- well, you forget to say that the Serbs had already broken up Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he didn't know what was going to happen with the Muslim-Serb relationship, and if anything were to happen, it wouldn't have been possible for him to defend Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. When President Tudjman says here, "Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be taken as something God given, which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is," are you saying that he, in fact, is telling us that the sovereignty -- the territorial integrity of Bosnia is something to be cherished and protected? It's quite the opposite, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The historical reflections of Franjo Tudjman were correct, there's no question about it, absolutely correct. And he quite clearly expressed them; that his political pragmatism, the fact that he was a realist, in political terms, in relation to the world he was in, well, made him say, Okay, this isn't fair. You beat us here, you diminished us here, you drove us out, you killed us, you conquered us as an imperial force, you looted us, but, very well, if we can prevent that, fine; if we can't prevent that, then we'll bow our heads and accept the political situation, such as it is. Yes, yes, I apologise. We'll accept the political situation, such as it is, and we will act as dictated by this lack of justice, not as dictated by justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I think you just hit the nail on the head when you talked about President Tudjman's pragmatism, political pragmatism. In fact, what's happening, given his very -- no one disputes his grasp and his deep knowledge of history. As a politician, what he sees is the disintegration of Yugoslavia as an opportunity for Croatia to right all the past wrongs, as he sees them and as you see them, past wrongs over the centuries against the Croatian people and the Croatian territories that they claim, and in fact this disintegration of Yugoslavia is now an opportunity to politically achieve something that would right all those past wrongs, and in fact that's going to involve pushing the borders of the Croatian state eastward to encompass the areas of the former banovina and to make those part of the Croatian state that he wishes to establish. Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. On page 100, the president says what the international community has to say. They are against modifying the borders. The president says that Lasic also says that tampering with the borders would open a Pandora's Box and we don't want this to happen. So they are opposed to changing the borders forcibly. President Tudjman also says that in Split he spoke to Izetbegovic tete-a-tete, and with Milosevic tete-a-tete, and also the three of them who held discussions, and they tried to find a solution. I quote. They tried to find a solution that would be satisfactory for the Serbian people, the Croatian people, and the Muslims. So they were looking for a satisfactory political solution for the three constituent peoples. They were looking for a peaceful solution. The borders were not to be changed by force. That was the Croatian position that was publicly adopted, and in secret. But if -- yes. Well, if we could have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got one more question and we'll be finished with this transcript, Mr. President, and then we can take the break, if I could ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 113. I've got one question to wrap up this meeting. Finally, after all this, after 113 pages of transcript, the president of the HDZ finally speaks up, Stjepan Kljujic, and he says: "After this, I can no longer occupy a post down there. I mean, we must be sincere. First, I am a private person. I could not be broken even during Communist times, when Branko Mikulic persecuted me ..." And the next paragraph, he says: "Well, let me tell you, regarding the policy here, it is not possible for the seventh dwarf to get up and make a ruckus about it. I did everything you told me to do. We cannot go on. You want Herceg-Bosna, you want Boban. Well, you're welcome to them, gentlemen. I resign. I am always ready to resign, Mr. President." Now, we know that despite those words, Kljujic continued in his position as president of the HDZ for a little while after this meeting, when he was then replaced by Miljenko Brkic and then subsequently by Mate Boban, but the last question I've got on this transcript, General, is that that really sums up the end result of this very important meeting on the 27th of December, 1991. It was Boban, Kordic, Kostroman, and Herceg-Bosna policy that eventually carried the day and won out. From this point, the -- those voices such as Ivan Markesic, Barac, Kljujic, the ones who sought a more conciliatory or moderate position in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina policy, they lost the battle here. Boban carried the day, and it was Boban, carrying out Tudjman's policy on Herceg-Bosna, that really was in effect from this moment, this day forward. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are your constructs, Mr. Stringer. We're speaking about a democratic party. Elections are held democratically, and Mr. Kljujic, who was a sports journalist before, a very decent gentleman with a bow 23 tie, he was so giving in to the positions of Mr. Izetbegovic, that Tudjman 24 said to him that Croats could not go to Serboslavia. There was a war on, and 25 Mr. Kljujic is engaged in speculative conversations, as Serbs occupy 70 per 1 cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The state, in reality, is no longer in 2 existence. It only exists on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We know what the situation is by now in Bosnia-Herzegovina at this time, so I think that you don't need to expound on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no more questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I have a few questions to ask you, Mr. Praljak, following the in-depth examination of this document of about 125 pages by Mr. Stringer. First of all, Mr. Praljak, I would like you to look at the last part of the document. You see that on the last page, it says that the meeting finished at 2155 hours and then they went for dinner, so I can only assume that their conversation must have carried on over dinner. Given Croat customs, do you have discussions of a professional nature during dinner or are you talking about the weather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with my experience, dinner gives rise to even more intensive discussion, so it gets even worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you can safely assume that discussions of a political nature that we see in this document carried on over dinner, and that we only have part of the discussion reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is highly probable that -- or practically certain that the political discussion continued over dinner. Probably the participants formed groups and tried to weigh their arguments. I'm sure that this was the case. It isn't the Croatian way, to have -- to have a conversation -- to engage in small talk over dinner, as the French. We're not at that level, psychologically, yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we look at this document, do you think that a conclusion could be drawn by everyone, including by yourself, and, namely, that within the Croat population of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a group which was perhaps against the ideas of Tudjman, and there was another group who seemed to be more inclined to be in line with Tudjman's ideas? Could we draw the conclusion that there were two groups, and one basically led by Mr. Kljujic, and in the other group we may have had Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree, Your Honour. There weren't -- there were not two groups there. Every area where Croats lived had its own problems; Posavina, Central Bosnia, Herzegovina, Sarajevo, so there was several groups and several political options. The clergy, on the one hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let's not go into this debate. If you do not like the word "group," could we perhaps say that there were two political options, the first one being represented by Mr. Kljujic and the second one by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. We may say that there is the political opinion of Mr. Kljujic which differs from that of Mr. Boban, but Kordic at that moment was not an important player, in the area of politics, to be the leader of any kind of political group, at least to my knowledge. But I think I have good knowledge of it, but conditionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we saw earlier on that Mr. Kljujic has decided to resign. It is very clear. If everyone agreed in the framework of a meeting, there would be no problem, but if, during a meeting, someone is handing down their resignation, it means that there is a problem. Don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the problem was explained by Mr. Kljujic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not in the way I would consider truthful. Mr. Kljujic tried to play an intellectual role to which he wasn't up to, in my opinion; namely, that everything be agreed in offices. And in the process, he failed to see the basic problems, and that is the total Serbian occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the splitting up of the country. And due to the encirclement of -- or, rather, the environment of Sarajevo, he didn't understand the policy of Alija Izetbegovic. He wanted to be an autonomous player and have others obey him. At such times, that wasn't possible, and that was held against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question for my part. I am thinking about all this, so this is not a statement, but looking at this document we see that, on the one hand, we have Mr. Tudjman explaining his understanding of the role that could be played by Croats of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the Republic of Croatia, or in a confederation type of state, or within the framework of an association of states -- and I will remind you, Mr. Praljak, that the Croat constitution and the constitution of the former Yugoslavia, as well as the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, provide for legal systems allowing this sort of solution. So as I was saying, when I see Mr. Tudjman explaining at length and going back to history and talking about banovina, and when I see also Mr. Tudjman stating, in a very clear manner, that the United States do not want any change in the borders, I'm wondering whether there is any compatibility between Mr. Tudjman's position which may be shared by others, others such as Kordic, Kostroman or others, with the position of the international community. I'm wondering how Mr. Tudjman could solve this problem, because we see at the beginning of the meeting he talks about the position of the United States, but at the same time it doesn't stop him from touching on the issue of borders, and this is what I don't manage to understand. Do you have an explanation that could help us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I can help you. He found a very clear solution to that situation by calling the Croats to go to a referendum and vote about an integral Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, two or three months after this meeting. Franjo Tudjman was fully aware of that. He only states a possibility here. If the United States agree, and the Muslims, and the Serbs, and it can all happen in a peaceful way, then we have a solution. But the subsequent events, the signed agreement, all show that this is a democratic and open putting forward of all options, and they can also be discussed openly, including things you don't want to try out, so just to see whether it makes sense, it's logical. I believe that the entire world functions like this. All governments put forward positions -- extreme positions, half extreme, logical, et cetera, and once you discuss all that, what follows is action. And from the actions, we can tell what is really happening. And the actions that followed, we know what they were like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Mr. Stringer asked you several questions regarding page 34, where Mr. Boban talks about border cleansing and talks about 60 per cent of the Croat population --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or 60 per cent Croat population, correction from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in Herceg-Bosna. This part of the transcript, as everyone understood, is very important, but I'm talking to a specialist in this field because you studied engineering, so I believe that you are very good at math. We know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croats made up 17 or 18 per cent of the population, but let's take 17 per cent. And, in fact, you said that the percentage was higher, but as time went by it decreased. You did not explain why there was a decrease. There could be various reasons linked to migration, linked to the economic situation. Perhaps Croats were looking for work abroad. In fact, you personally went abroad, especially in Germany, which could explain why the percentage decreased to 17 per cent. But what I would like to know is the following: With a population of 17 per cent, how could Mr. Boban say that, In some regions we would move to 65 per cent? With what method could he come to this percentage? Of course you heard Mr. Stringer, according to him, it could be the consequence of ethnic cleansing, stating that by dealing with the -- by removing the Muslims, we would come to this percentage. But is it as simple as that? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not at all the way it was stated here. It's completely different. Mr. Boban initially says the following: These municipalities that are at the foundation of HZ-HB, so these being as they were, according to the census in that area, there are 55 per cent of Croats, 27 per cent of Muslims, twenty – nine per cent of Serbs, and the rest is accounted for by others living there. And now we arrive at the following. One of the insidious aspects of the system in which we lived was the reorganisation of municipalities in such a way that one municipality, if it had been normally established, there would have been 52 per cent of Croats, but then you add to it a part of another municipality, a territory, and there are, say, a number of villages inhabited exclusively by Muslims. Thus, you reduce the share of Croats in that municipality to, say, 35 per cent. This is how the municipalities in Croatia were established in order to have a Serb majority or a relative majority in some municipalities in Croatia, and that's how municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were established to get a Muslim or Serb majority in some municipalities. And Mate Boban says here if we were to remove these parts of municipalities at the brink of these municipalities which were joined by Rankovic and Pozderac and others, and if we were to re-establish the municipalities in a natural way, then in that same HZ-HB, there would be not 55 per cent of Croats, but due to this elimination of joined villages or towns, the absolute number of Croats would remain the same, but their relative share would rise from 55 per cent to 65 per cent. This is what this says explicitly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what you are saying here is news to me, because until now I had not understood that municipalities had been rearranged in their delineation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and by having a re-delineation of the borders of municipalities, some populations had been transferred from one municipality to another on paper. So if what you say is true, when did this restructuring happen or this new carving up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatia, that happened right after the Second World War, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially as regards the Serb side, also after the Second World War. As regards the 1980s, or the late 1970s or early 1980s, while Hamdija Pozderac, a Muslim Communist politician was in power, that was done. Let's take Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have the 1991 census, so it is based on the census results that questions were raised until now both by the Prosecutor and by the Defence counsels. So let's talk about this 1991 census. It basically sets out the population make-up; Serbs, Croats, Muslims. Based on that, everyone is working on the municipalities, so there has not been a new carving up of the municipalities before that census, or has there been one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the municipalities were re-delineated earlier. That's what happened to the Travnik municipality, to a large extent this applies to Mostar also. And besides that, Your Honour, the 1991 census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, thank you. I understood very well. I'm sorry if I'm being very brief, but I want to give the floor back to Mr. Stringer as soon as possible. If I understood correctly, because everything is quite complex and we must try and avoid to look at those things in a very broad brush, when Mr. Boban talks about 65 per cent of the Croat population in Herceg-Bosna, according to you, does he have in mind the new delineation of municipalities which took place after the Second World War, which means that there was some changes in the ethnic make-up, which means that he wants to go back to the situation that they had at the end of the Second World War? Is that what you're trying to make us understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. He wants the municipalities to be re-delineated to the state before the new delineation by Hamdija Pozderac, and that would have increased the relative share of the Croats from 55 to 65 per cent; no cleansing, no driving out of people. In one part of the transcript, a municipality is mentioned where this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in Mr. Boban's intervention, in English it says "cleansing," which is quite a troublesome word. In the B/C/S version, the original version, what word does he use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, it's the word "ciscenje," "cleansing," which has a very negative or awkward meaning, but the previous sentence explains what it's about. Because the word "composing" is used, if I were to compose this audience, I could make it up of more or fewer women, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I go back to what was said before, in your language, and please apologise for my pronunciation, is "ciscenje." This is what we see on line 23, page 46. But he seemed to be saying that, according to him, it meant a new carving up of municipal borders. But this word, as it is in the transcript, is it a word of a general meaning or is there a connotation of cleansing, which means that when you clean, you remove; whereas, in a new municipal carving up or delineation, you are not removing anything, you are basically drawing new municipal borders on a map, you are carving up a new map for political reasons or for other reasons without having to remove or to practice any cleansing? So the word that has been used, which has a connotation that no one can deny, because when you talk about cleansing, you immediately think of ethnic cleansing, so I was wondering whether this word in your language is used in a general context or is it very targeted to a specific action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Croatian language, just as in any other language, the meaning of a word is determined by the context. It is correct, Your Honour, that this word in Croatian, too, is used in the sense cleanse a suit, clean a window. It mostly has a technical meaning, clean up a room, clean -- to clean or cleanse the air. But due to the subsequent events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it got connotations which it used not to have in Croatian. Now, of course, as any other word, it gets a sense which was additionally added, and that's the sense of ethnic cleansing. So whenever you see the word "cleansing," which was used before the ethnic cleansing, you immediately think of ethnic cleansing, but here this does not apply. Here, they are speaking about changing municipality borders, because if you add Citluk and Siroki Brijeg to Mostar, then Mostar will be 60 or 70 per cent Croatian, but if you take it -- take some parts away from it, it will be different. That's how things were done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask two, as it were, negative questions, but first: Did you read the whole transcript here, did you read this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right, and you can certainly help me. I have missed, in the discussions here, what we have seen, any reference, one, to an attack by the ABiH, and that came later, in fact; is that correct?
