utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is 1991. The attack of the Army of BiH only started in the spring of 1993. I mean, they are centuries apart, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second reference that I think was not made here, there is no reference to the fact that the Sarajevo government does not work, that it's not a functioning government. This is not used as an argument for the creation of Herceg-Bosna in this transcript, in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on a few of the points raised by His Honour. General, we're just talking about this word "cleanse" as it's used in Croatian. When he said "cleanse the border areas," what Boban was invoking was an idea of cleansing by which one rids oneself of something which is undesirable, to clean or to wash, a window, a piece of clothing, something that has a spot or is dirty, and what needs to happen is that that needs to be cleansed; that is, the undesirable parts of that need to be gotten rid of. I mean, isn't that the idea that he's invoking here, and the undesirable thing being that of Muslims or non-Croats in this area of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. He's speaking about areas. If he had wanted to say, We'll cleanse the Muslims, he would have said so. But then why only from border areas? Why not from all areas? He's speaking about the areas of municipalities that were unnaturally and intentionally added in a politically rotten way to enable a people to be the majority in a municipality which it normally wouldn't have. That's a problem which I know well; how, by changing municipality borders, one people was put in a position to dominate another. And he's saying, Let's get rid of these border areas, and not, We'll expel the Muslims. And that same Mate Boban later had 10.000 Muslims in the HVO, and then there were refugees, et cetera. So come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting, General, that -- so what Boban is proposing here, if I understand you correctly, is that they're going to go in -- the Herceg-Bosna people are going to redraw the borders of the various municipalities in Herceg-Bosna, and to do it in a way that guarantees that the Croats are a majority in each of these areas, each of these municipalities, and that that's all going to be done, and the Muslims are going to be okay with that even in a municipality like Jablanica, where they form nearly 70 per cent of the population, that they're just going to stand by and watch while Boban and his people gerrymander and rig the borders of the municipalities to create a bunch of Croatian majorities that didn't previously exist; is that what you're saying was going to happen, and this was all going to happen peacefully?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, it wasn't that way. You cannot change the number of -- or you can't change the population in Jablanica. But by adding Muslim villages to Prozor and Rama in an unnatural way, you can raise the number of Muslims there, and by adding those villages to the Jablanica municipality, you can raise the number of Muslims in that municipality. A compact territory was split up between other municipalities, and Mate Boban says that possibly this can be done based on certain conditions, et cetera. So it's about that. So if we want to go into that, I can tell you about the gerrymandering of municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have seen an example in this transcript what this was like. But nobody is saying that the number of Muslims in Jablanica can be reduced, but it can be increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've mentioned the refugees, and we're going to get to that later, because we're just talking about December of 1991, before the war has come to Bosnia and Herzegovina, before the referendum on independence, before the encirclement of Sarajevo that you were invoking earlier in your testimony in response to Judge Antonetti's question. And, in fact, the Serbian occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the encirclement, the siege of Sarajevo, none of that was happening in December of 1991, was it? That came some months later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was encircled several months later, but the occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the JNA, and the weapons handed out to the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had already taken place to a large extent. As you know, the JNA had taken over all areas around Mostar. People had been killed, there was shooting from the hills at the time, and the international community requested that the JNA leave Croatia and Slovenia, and their troops went to Bosnia and Herzegovina; the Rijeka Corps, the Ljubljana Corps, numerous people, many weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Also in response to a question, the President was discussing the statement of Stjepan Kljujic at the Presidential meeting, the Presidential transcript, and the President suggested or indicated that the problem -- this is line 8 on page 41: "And the problem was explained by Mr. Kljujic, wasn't it?" And what you said was: "Well, not in the way I would consider truthful." So now we've been -- we've been on this cross-examination, General, for almost a week, and I'm counting now four people who you call to be -- you claim are untruthful or are liars because what they're saying doesn't coincide with your world-view; former President Mesic, Major Boricic, who was a major with the training organ of the Croatian Army. He wrote the report on the deployment of the 5th Guards Brigade in Herceg-Bosna that we were talking about earlier. You said he wrote a false report or his numbers were not correct and truthful. You said the same thing about Brigadier Kapular, the commander of the 5th Guards Brigade. You said he submitted a false report to Croatian Defence Minister Susak. And now it's Kljujic who's not being truthful in this conversation when he's characterising the events taking place in this conversation. So that's how it is, isn't it, General, that whenever someone says something, however many years ago, before this Tribunal was even up and running, whenever someone said something that doesn't coincide with your testimony, you claim that that person is a liar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, that's not true. I didn't say that Brigadier Kapular was lying. All I know is the precise reason for which he doctored the report sent to Gojko Susak. I know the precise reason. It's because he wanted more boots, more weapons, because he had a poor army that was poorly equipped, so he changed the figures a bit. Please allow me to answer. And Stipe Mesic, on page 41 and 42, in the entire transcript that consists of 115 pages, he says -- I haven't said anything about Mesic. If Mr. Mesic is discussing division here, and he was aware of what was going on in Karadjordjevo, why doesn't he state that here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Stringer is conducting his cross-examination, he's putting the questions. Therefore, answer his question precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I put the Mesic testimony in front of you. You were invited to comment on it. We're done with that. The same with Kapular and the others. What I'm pointing out here is the fact that you claim -- you're very quick to claim others are lying when whatever they say is inconsistent with what you say, so we don't need to go back into the merits of Mesic's testimony on Karadjordjevo. Now, one last point on this, and again this is a response you gave to the questions from Judge Antonetti --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's your question, what's your question? That you're saying that I am saying that Kapular is lying? What's the question? And that you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've clarified that for us. You said that he doctored -- he submitted a doctored report to the minister of defence. So that is noted in the record, and I'm ready to move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, well, then don't repeat your thesis. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said, in response to a question from Judge Antonetti about Kljujic, you said he wanted to be an autonomous player and have others obey him. At such times, that wasn't possible, and that was held against him. You just said that a few minutes ago on page 41 of the transcript, and that was -- the fact that he wanted to be autonomous, the fact that he wanted to be the president of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was his undoing, wasn't it, because, in fact, it was President Tudjman who was going to be the one calling the shots on HDZ policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the fact that Kljujic wanted to be autonomous was inconsistent with what Tudjman's views are, and that's why the puppet, his puppet, Boban, was ultimately installed, who was anything but autonomous and whose sole purpose was to do the opposite? His purpose was to implement policy and to take instructions from President Tudjman. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That's without any basis, it's illogical, it's absurd, it's something that has just been fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, General. We're going to skip ahead in time. We've been talking about this conversation in the Presidential Palace on the 27th of December, 1991. We're going to skip ahead about 18 months. P02719, it's another Presidential transcript. It's a conversation taking place on the 11th of June, 1993, and it's a conversation between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I just want to take you to one part of this quickly. We'll come back to this transcript later, but the point I want to raise with you now is on page 14, it starts on page 14, where Izetbegovic is complaining to President Tudjman about some of the conduct and activities of Boban and others in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on page 14, Izetbegovic says, bottom half: "UNPROFOR's official statement was that the weather was bad, that they could not go ..." He's talking, I believe, about a meeting with Boban that did not come to pass. He continues: "... that's what we heard that day and later too; and then we heard that Boban claimed how he had been shot at. As for Boban's statements, you can believe him. I have the right not to believe him. I have a hundred reasons not to believe him. Boban is constantly stirring up quarrels down there; you have to know that. I have to tell you that. You can believe me or not, that is up to you, but you have to know that he and several other people are behind those conflicts down there." And then President Tudjman asks: "Who else, in your opinion?" And Izetbegovic mentions, on the next page: "Kordic, Kostroman, from Busovaca, and he, these three, four people." Tudjman says: "So the ones who were defending Busovaca are in your --" And then Izetbegovic cuts him off. He says: "You know, if there are a hundred people here and if two of them were to tell you that this man Kordic is smart, do not defend him, you can defend anyone." And Tudjman says: "I am not defending him at all." And Izetbegovic continues talking about Kordic. And I'm going to move across to page 16, and Tudjman says: "You mentioned Kostroman. Where is he and what is he?" Izetbegovic says: "I think he is in Kiseljak or in Busovaca, in those parts, anyway." And Izetbegovic says, quote -- sorry, President Tudjman says: "Mr. Izetbegovic, I neither knew or appointed Boban, Kordic or Kostroman. These people emerged, appeared down there during the defence against the Serbian aggression. The only message they were receiving from us in Zagreb was to cooperate with you, which is what I also recommended to you, asking you to establish cooperation." Now, we've just finished looking at this transcript from 27th of December, 1991 - Tudjman, Kordic, Kostroman, Boban - the others, where Tudjman talks at length about how Bosnia-Herzegovina is not God given, how it's not in Croatia's interests that it be preserved, making those statements directly as the president of the Republic of Croatia to these gentlemen, Boban, Kordic, Kostroman. And then what we see here is Tudjman not telling the truth to Izetbegovic, telling Izetbegovic something completely different, telling Izetbegovic that, in fact, his message to them is to cooperate with Izetbegovic. Now, he was misleading Izetbegovic at best, wasn't he? He was concealing from Izetbegovic the true nature of the instructions and the relationship between Tudjman, Boban, Kordic, and Kostroman; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you're claiming is totally absurd. Between this period and the other one, well, more than a year and a half had passed. In the meantime, Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised by Croatia after the referendum had been held. I don't know how you want to understand the policies. In such difficult times, no one knew anything. Well, these weren't positions. These were discussions, Mr. Stringer. There are no positions expressed there, no conclusions. After Izetbegovic had taken Travnik and had appointed his generals, after he had ruined Konjic and killed people, after his army had killed people, after Kakanj had been taken, after Zenica had been cleansed, in the midst of Zagreb he lied to Tudjman. Izetbegovic lied to Tudjman. These were pure lies, and this is what he would always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, what we see here, and since you've used the word, General, Tudjman lied to Izetbegovic here, didn't he, when he told Izetbegovic that his message to Kordic and Kostroman and to Boban was to cooperate, when, in fact, his message was the opposite, and the policies of Herceg-Bosna were the opposite as well; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, that was not the case. Otherwise, how would the Croats have voted in the referendum? You're really trying to depict me as someone whose IQ is 80 or 82, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think my IQ is lower, Judge Trechsel? Is that what you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm -- I have no thoughts about your IQ. Maybe I do not have the same view of it that you have, but that's not the subject here. But I find your response to Mr. Stringer -- I cannot follow. Mr. Stringer puts it to you that at one point, as we have seen in a document, Tudjman had said one thing, and then at another point in time and to other interlocutors, he says something else. And he asks you whether you see a contradiction, and instead you pretend that you are taken for unintelligent. I do not see any -- I simply cannot follow you. I don't understand what you're trying to say, except that I do not see that you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying, in answer to the question, that at the meeting no conclusions were presented. Everything was stated in conditional. Certain thoughts were expressed, thoughts and positions of a political kind. And from that point in time, what happened is what we have seen in hundreds of documents in this court. There were refugees, there was the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. So linking this up, well, I don't understand it, but I'll answer the question. Mr. Stringer, I fully disagree with your conclusions. I fully disagree with your conclusions and theories. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. The next exhibit is 1D00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, we have just seen this document, which is a conversation between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman on the 11th of June. The document doesn't state where this took place. I assume that this was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Zagreb. It's a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, in Zagreb. I noticed that the conversation started off at 1.00 in the morning, approximately, 25 minutes past midnight. The topic must have certainly been important. But after midnight in Croatia, in the various administrations, was there always a civil servant there who was ready to record the conversations? Since you attended these meetings in this office or meeting room where these meetings took place, was it in Mr. Tudjman's office, was this in a meeting room? And we saw a photograph of this. Whether it was in a meeting room or in an office, a recording procedure is something quite specific. You need everything to be ready. Were they able to record this conversation after midnight? In logistical terms, this has been to be organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. Very often, President Tudjman would call you at 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning and ask you to come. We were at war, we were creating a state. Everyone was prepared to react at any time, 24 hours a day. At least those in my circle couldn't act as if they had specific working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is 1D00401. This is an excerpt of a book written by Dr. Tudjman in 1981, this book entitled "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe." And I'm looking at page --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not receiving any interpretation into the Croatian language, so could -- or we don't have a translation into the Croatian language, so could the Prosecutor please read out slowly so that it can be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I want to have the Croatian version. This is an academic book, and I need to have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, Mr. Praljak would like to leave the courtroom for a few minutes. He needs to leave the room. This is an important document we have before us, since it stems from Mr. Tudjman, and it is in English. The accused is entitled to have any document in his own language when it is part of his trial. Maybe you have a translation of this document into B/C/S. Perhaps you have. You could then address this document after our break or in August, when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's a 1D document. It's admitted into evidence, and at the moment I cannot tell you whether it's been -- there's got to be a B/C/S version out there somewhere, because I doubt that President Tudjman wrote the book in English. So we're going to check, and I can skip over this for the time being. Perhaps counsel for Mr. Prlic can shed some light.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this book is concerned, a Croatian version certainly exists, but we received the English version of the book. We don't have the Croatian version. Since we've worked with this book with Ambassador Sancevic, or we used this book with Ambassador Sancevic, it wasn't a problem for him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This book must have been published in the Croatian language. Clearly, the Prlic Defence team has been using the English version of the book. I would like to draw your attention to the title of the book, "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe." You are certainly going to be using this to present your case, so it would only be fair for Mr. Praljak to be able to read the entire book before purposefully answering your question. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. This exhibit was used by the Prlic Defence on the direct examination of their witness, Ambassador Sancevic. Apparently it didn't cause any problems at the time, as counsel's indicated. I think I came back to it also with Ambassador Sancevic on the cross-examination. If the general wants to look off of an original language version, he's certainly entitled to do that, and I can pass over this document for the time being and move on, and we'll see if we can find these pages in the original language version. If so, then I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move on to another document, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we've been talking a lot about the meetings with President Tudjman, his meetings with Boban and the others, meetings taking place in Zagreb, events taking place there. I want to bring this down to events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and try and get this closer down to the ground level and out of the Presidential offices in Zagreb. And in order to do that, I want to take you to the testimony from Mr. Vulliamy, who was the journalist with "The Guardian," who testified in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we have an excerpt of his testimony in Sanction, Mr. President, that we can put on the screen so others can follow along. Page 1499 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And beginning on line 16, Mr. Vulliamy is asked: "Do you recall any of the events that happened when you met with Mr. Mate Boban?" And we're going to go through a little bit this meeting which occurred in August of 1992. He says on line 18: "Yes. I recall -- I recall the meeting well." This is Vulliamy meeting with Boban in August of 1992: "It was at his office in a town called Grude, a small town and quite a menacing place, although there was no actual fighting there." It goes down -- I'm going to skip over some lines. He says, on line 24: "... Mate Boban was very much the name that one associated with the apex of power among the Bosnian Croats." And on to page 1500 of the transcript, I'm going to move to line 10. He's asked the approximate date of the meeting he had with Mr. Boban. On line 10, Mr. Vulliamy says: "Well, it would have been -- it would have to be approximate, I'm afraid. It's -- travelled on the 12th. It's the -- just before the middle of August. If I can guess it, it's 12, 13, 14th of August, something of that area. "Q. Of which year? "A. 1992." And then Mr. Vulliamy was asked to recount his recollection of the meeting on plans for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and Vulliamy says: "Yes --" line 19: "He made it clear and he was, incidentally, willing and wanting to have this conversation. He made it clear that he did not and could not recognise the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor could he recognise Sarajevo as its capital. The reason he gave was that the constitution guaranteed the rights of individuals, but not of people, and the word he used for people was 'narod,' which is an important word because it means people as an ethnicity or it is -- does it mean people going shopping? It means a people, the 'Hrvatski Narod,' the Croatian people ." This is page 1501, line 3: "He then went on to describe in some detail how he wanted the various 'narod,' Serbian, Muslims and Croatians, to be divided within Bosnia by a system of what he called cantons or provinces, which he likened, I think, for sort of public relations reasons, to Switzerland and the European Union, and how one group of these cantons or provinces would be specifically Croatian. He talked about how Herceg-Bosna was connected to Croatia, and the words he used were culturally, spiritually, economically, and he said that it -- that Herceg-Bosna had been separated from Croatia by what he called 'unfortunate historical circumstances.' And he then talked about the HVO as specifically -- he didn't -- he didn't talk about the HVO in relation to the HDZ, to his party, but he talked about them as the legitimate military force on what he called the free territory, and went on to make some remark that -- of a nature that the Croatian people were ready to arm to defend this freedom, as he put it, which was language which my experience told me was not always defensive." Now, two questions on this for you, General. First of all, Boban's views, expressed to Mr. Vulliamy in this conversation in August of 1992, are essentially a mirror image of the views of President Tudjman, aren't they, these cultural and spiritual links between Herceg-Bosna, Croatia, and the unfortunate historical circumstances that resulted in separation from Croatia? So wouldn't you agree with me, based on what we've seen already, that Boban's views were essentially the same views as President Tudjman on this issue?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm in an awkward situation here. I don't know -- I don't know how I can answer to such a question. These are the positions of Mate Boban he put forward at a meeting with Mr. Vulliamy. I don't know what they spoke about. I only know what Vulliamy says that they spoke about. But based on this account, I can say that everything is all right. Vulliamy just says that Grude is a frightening place, which is very English, a very English thing to say. That is correct that the notion of "narod," "people," is not defined in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it was defined in the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that there are peoples that have an original sovereignty. And then Boban speaks about cantons. This idea was present all the time in our minds. Why not have a political system such as in Switzerland? There, they also had a civil war, and eventually they came up with cantons. Boban speaks about cultural and economic links between Croats that live in two countries, but that can be said for all of Europe. Why shouldn't the cultural and economic links be boosted? And I don't know Vulliamy's experience, but the HVO, by that time, had already defended Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Serbian Army, lest they should be overrun, and I don't see any -- anything here that is -- I don't see any contradiction there. So a cantonal system, as in Switzerland, et cetera, and about the experience of Mr. Vulliamy and his way of interpreting a certain word, well, that's up to him. That's his right as a journalist, and no one is denying him that right. I only know what our positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, General, I take it from what you're saying, that the views here expressed by Mr. Boban were not only the views voiced by President Tudjman, as we've seen in the earlier transcripts, but that he's essentially setting out views that are consistent with your own -- your own position, in terms of the establishment of a canton or an area that would be specifically Croatian within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically Croatian. So, yes, today, Mr. Stringer, even today I claim that the cantonal system is the best system for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even now I say that the HVO was a regular defence force that saved Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I still think that the Swiss model, if the European communities had adopted it and imposed it, would have been the best. The Croats wanted nothing but equality with other peoples and the protection of their national and sovereign interests, and I still think that we must develop cultural relations with everybody. And what Mate Boban thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look and see what you said on this same subject some years ago. I've got a video-clip that I'm going to play for you. It's P0 -- or it's from P09447, and this is the documentary "Death of Yugoslavia." Do you remember giving these interviews to the journalist for this programme on the death of Yugoslavia, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. Just tell me the year. It wasn't a few years ago. Please be precise about the date when this was made. Let's be precise here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was going to ask you if you could tell me the year. Let's play the video, and then we'll see how much you remember about it. Let's go ahead and start it, then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your evidence, so please tell me when this was made. Enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not getting sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we're waiting for this video, I believe that the general has the absolute right to know the time when this was made, because we have already heard from him that he is not certain of dates and years, so he cannot say precisely. And apart from that, he has a right to know when this was made. Whenever we submitted a document or a video, we had to state when and where it was made, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, do you have the dates? Are you going to give it later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't have the date handy, Mr. President. I can provide it after the break. I think the plan was to ask the general if he recognises this. I don't think that there's much dispute about his face appearing on the screen. I think the normal procedure is to have him look at it and see if he can tell us if he remembers when he gave these interviews. I can supply the date, Mr. President, and I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a certain likeness between this man and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're not getting the sound. Perhaps we could take our break a little bit early. We could fix the sound and I could come back with the date of the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have our break now, and perhaps you can sort this technical hitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I hope that the video is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm told the video is working, and I can provide the Trial Chamber and the parties with this information, and also the general. The interviews of General Praljak that are shown on this are from April of 1995. The interviews form part of what I believe is a well-known BBC production called "The Death of Yugoslavia" which accompanied or is also the name of a well-known book by Laura Silver and Alan Little, entitled also "The Death of Yugoslavia." The BBC documentary, the film part, was broadcast for the first time in September of 1995, and I've been told that the actual footage here of the interviews with General Praljak were received by the Office of the Prosecutor and me on the 14th of April, 1998. I had forgotten that, but apparently my name is the name that's on our internal documentation as being the recipient, probably the requester of the video. So again, General, the interviews are from April 1995. The broadcast was in September of 1995. The footage received by the Office of the Prosecutor, 14th of April, 1998. So, General, let's -- let's just run this, and we can then talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, beneath the image there is a text, but we're not getting interpretation and there is no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, I've called the technician and he'll be in here in a minute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's skip over to P00466. I think everyone will be happy to go to another Presidential transcript while we're waiting for the problem to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, can you take P00466 in your binder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're moving ahead in time a bit from the December 1991 Presidential transcript that we talked about earlier today. This is now September 11th of 1992, and this is the first session of the National Defence Council, Republic of Croatia, and you are present at this meeting, General, along with Gojko Susak and others, as indicated on the cover page. And at one point during the questions that Judge Antonetti was putting to you earlier, you were asked about something on page 54, and so I would like to take you to that for clarification. Actually, yeah, turning to page 54 to 57. Actually, General, forgive me. Let's go back to page 51, because since we're having all these other technical problems I'll maybe take a few extra minutes with this transcript. On page 51, again this is September of 1992, so this is not long before the events in Prozor that we know about, and also the fall of Jajce, and about halfway down the page you say: "And war with the Muslims can be anticipated." Susak says: "We have been aware of that for over a week now, and we made preparations on what needs to be done." And then, General, you state: "We have six dead on the post. The situation is culminating, the roads are blocked now down there. Tonight they will let some through. They are not letting through, right or left. The people have just calmed down not to go through -- the people have just calmed down not to go through right away. That is one problem." And then you continue and you say: "Another problem is that the Serbs, with their way of solving the Muslim issue, have put us in the position where we will lose everything we defended because the Muslims will settle in there. We are left a minority everywhere except in the part of Western Herzegovina. And that, I think, needs to be a special subject for talks, with precise political decisions on how to solve that." There is a passage, though: "Not everyone is always benignant," which I would suggest in English is "benign," perhaps, "but they are not too bad either. And there it seems, if you want, I have -- I wouldn't want any -- I wouldn't want to be annoying, but if tonight it's late, then whenever and wherever." So here what you're doing is, and you've talked about this in your testimony, General, the problem now that's developing with the arrival of a large number of Muslim refugees into Herceg-Bosna from areas they've been driven away from by the Serbs, so carrying on from what we were talking about earlier, in addition to the sort of natural or the flow -- the downward trend of Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna, by the latter part of 1992 the situation was much worse because of Muslim refugees arriving from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was disastrous. It was not merely worse. The reduction in percentages as a consequence of what had happened, the Serbs from 70 per cent of the territory that they had occupied by that time, had expelled Muslims and Croats. The Croats went to Croatia; Muslims, too, but a large number didn't only settle in Herceg-Bosnia, but also other free territory not occupied by the Serbs, and that had caused a disastrous situation. It was a complete disaster, and this was a very strong impetus to change the situation, political and psychological, in the Muslims. All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it was a disaster on a number of different levels. Clearly, it was a humanitarian disaster and placed a tremendous burden not only on the refugees who were arriving, but also the people who had been living in these areas their entire lives. So we can agree that there was a humanitarian disaster in the making; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, humanitarian, social, psychological, and every other aspect. It was an extremely chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the Croatian policy vis-a-vis Herceg-Bosna, it was a political disaster because now this desire or this objective to create a Croatian space, canton, area, was tremendously more complicated now by the fact that the numbers, in terms of demographics, were swinging even greater in the wrong direction for you, in that the Muslim numbers were increasing. Isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a human disaster. It's a disaster for the entire people. And in such a situation, of course, it's a national disaster because the Croats are then wiped out from these areas. The same as happened in Sarajevo, which now is 96 per cent Muslim. It's not a political disaster, because nobody wanted to separate anything. This is -- this is a pure disaster which topples any sort of a rational system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But as the number of Muslims living in these parts of Herceg-Bosna increases, there is a corresponding decrease in the possibility of a political solution where there is going to be -- this is going to be a Croatian space in which Croatians are the majority. I mean, that's pure mathematics; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is pure mathematics. If somebody takes 500 million people from somewhere else to America, then the question will be raised: Whose is America? So if you settle an area for hundreds of years and then somebody expels the people from there, and nobody reacts, and now we speak about I don't know what, and back then everybody watched on coolly how a human disaster, above all human, was unfolding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, moving on to page 54, you say: "Listen, we are done for, we've lost. Listen, first the bloodshed is going to happen. I don't know what, and we will come into the same position as the Serbs. All this has to be left. There are cases of dysentery and refugee camps and the West. And then later if the West manages to get the territories from where the Serbs had expelled them, let them return there. "Because since we cannot," and then there's a word missing, "refugee problem here, our people, to the places they fled from, there's no theoretical chance in Bosnia we will lose. We don't stand a chance to defend it." And now what you're saying here, General, is the fact that with this influx of Muslims into Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian lands of Herceg-Bosna, that really there isn't going to be any way to achieve this Croatian space, territory, that you and the others advocate, at least not as long as all these Muslim refugees continue to live there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. Here I'm speaking as a sociologist who has read everything from August Comte to Durkheim and Weber, and more recent authors know what happens in such situations. This is a classical scientific analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, I'm asking you not about what others have written about sociology. I'm asking you specifically about this Herceg-Bosna territory. In order to achieve this Croatian space, this canton, whatever you want to call it, the problem that you faced at this point, that you're highlighting here, is that you've got too many Muslim refugees, too many Muslim people, present in this area, and that you're not going to be able to achieve that Croatian canton or territory because all of those people now have arrived; isn't that true? The numbers are undermining your objectives in establishing Croatian space?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We were not creating a Croatian space. We wanted to establish the conditions that existed before the war, and I'm saying here that the war changed the ethnic composition, that this area was ethnically occupied, and you are insinuating when you're saying that we want a pure Croatian space. I'm just saying that international law and the great powers must do what they can for the -- to enable the refugees to return from where they had come from. That was their duty, but it was not fulfilled to this day, as we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, President Tudjman begins speaking, and he says: "We do have a chance, in the sense that we will say what we said in the beginning. We have to, and we will insist on the request that the areas which used to be within the Croatian Banovina were demographically and geopolitically part of Croatia. "Accordingly, all those changes we created by the war." It might actually be "were created by the war." So I'm going to skip over, and I'm going to get back to the text that Judge Antonetti brought you to earlier during his questioning, and this is on page 56. And President Tudjman says: "Gentlemen, gentlemen, let's not orient. We have nothing to conquer. Let's defend --" This is about halfway down the page: "Gentlemen, gentlemen, let's not orient. We have nothing to conquer --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 56. Are you with me, General? He says: "Let's not orient. We have nothing to conquer. Let's defend those Croatian --" You interject, General, and you say: "Nowhere, Mr. President, it is impossible to pass further." And President Tudjman says: "And let's get ready to cleanse them out of Croatia. As I said, do not get involved in conquering Bosnia." And you say at the top of page 57: "No, Mr. President, believe me, the attacks have stopped." And then Minister Susak says: "Nothing out of Banovina, we did not trespass, not even one metre." Now, this discussion, General, what's happening here is that President Tudjman is yet again defining the Croatian territory -- Croatian space as being that of encompassing the Banovina territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what he's telling you and what he's telling Minister Susak is that that is the outside limit -- that's the limit of the area that you are going to defend, if I can put it that way. So what, in effect, is happening here is that you're all agreeing that you're going to fight for the Banovina, despite the tremendous amount of aggression and offensive action being taken by Serbs at this very point in time throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. The president's instructions to you, accepted by you and Susak, are that what you're going to defend is Croatia, and for you Croatia means Banovina, and you're not going to take one step out of the Banovina, but you're going to defend the Banovina, as opposed to defending the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, isn't that the correct interpretation of what's being discussed here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially correct, but you have skipped significant parts of the transcript. Prior to this, we had a large-scale operation against the Serbs in the Neretva Valley, and this was referred to here. And there is no good reason for us to attack the Serbs, Trebinje, Nevesinje, which is where they were in an absolute majority. We didn't want war. We wanted to defend ourselves. We weren't an offensive army. Franjo Tudjman, when someone from the international community thought they'd stop the Serbs, well, as he says on page 41, at the bottom, well, he says he's interested in us not conquering anything. Banovina, well, this wasn't created because Croatia wanted to expand, but this was inhabited by Croats mostly, and Muslims and other people too, and we defended this. We weren't interested in conquering Banja Luka. We proposed a peaceful solution when we defended this, and those policies were correct, quite peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General. So what you're going to defend is the Croatian territory as delimited by the Banovina. You're not interested in doing anything to move the Serbs out of Nevesinje, Trebinje, for example, which is the place where all these Muslims have been expelled. You're only interested in Croat space. You're not interested in restoring territory -- free territory to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. You shouldn't refer to Croatia, because it's not Croatia that is concerned. In Mostar, there weren't only Croats whom we were defending. In Stolac, there weren't only Croats either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, let me cut you off there --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're telling us this doesn't concern Croatia, but we're talking about a conversation that's taking place here in the office of the president of the Republic of Croatia. It's a conversation in which the participants are the president of Croatia, the defence minister of the Croatian Army, and you, who is in the process of being sent down to command HVO forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the same time that you're an assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia and a member of this National Security Council or National Defence Council that's been convened here. So it's a bit untrue, isn't it, General, to say that this isn't about Croatia? In fact, it's all about Croatia, and it's all about Croatia's policy in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I don't know how this was interpreted, when it says it doesn't concern Croatia. I didn't say that. That's the first thing. That from the 11th of September, that's the date of the conversation, in 1992, and the 24th of July, 1993, when I became the commander, well, you said, You were in the process of becoming a commander, well, this is nonsensical. This was a lot later, and many things had changed by then. I'm only disputing your claim that this is Croatian territory. It was the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, mainly inhabited by Croats, but there were also many Muslims who were in the HVO, in the armija, and there were many other peoples too. And first we didn't want to expel the Serbs from Nevesinje, and we didn't have the forces to do that either, Mr. Stringer, with such an ABiH that didn't attack Serbs, hit the Serbs anyway. We didn't have the force. We wouldn't launch an attack. We were defending an area, and at this time we attempted to launch a large-scale attack against the Serbs and it was partially successful. The Army of Republika Srpska was very strong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to make a correction. The accused previously said "it is not Croatia," not "it doesn't concern Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, maybe you and I are talking at cross-purposes here. Maybe we don't understand each other about what is Bosnia-Herzegovina and what is Croatia. If you look at the bottom of page 56, when President Tudjman says, Let's get ready to cleanse them out of Croatia, do not get involved in conquering Bosna, President Tudjman's Croatia and your Croatia was not only the Republic of Croatia but also the Banovina area within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it? I mean, that's what Croatia is for all of you, is Croatia plus Banovina; isn't that what he's saying here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when he says -- when Susak says, then, on page 57: "Nothing out of Banovina," he's not talking about only defending Croatian territory that you thought of as Croatia, which was the Banovina region in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's pretty evident, isn't it, General, that when they talk about Croatia, they're talking about -- or they're including the Banovina region of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you can have any impression you like. That's -- those are your charges, and they're nonsensical, but they're -- there's no word of this. As far as Croatia is concerned, Franjo Tudjman says that Croatia quite simply became, well, a place where anyone could do what they wanted to do. That's contained in another transcript. We had, in fact, become a house without a boss. Everyone was walking around with arms, and the Muslims were active, obtaining weapons, and so on and so forth. So my answer to your question is that what you are saying makes no sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So I've put to you the Prosecution's view or its interpretation of these words here. You don't accept them, so we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unless there's a question from the Chamber, Mr. President, I've got --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But have a look at page 57, where Franjo Tudjman says, Well, we don't want the Islamic people to say that we are the aggressor in Bosnia, that we're conquering in Bosnia, so that's why you shouldn't attack. The world says, We're accusing you of an attack, and so on and so forth. Mr. Stringer, you're extracting sentences. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we get the last word interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to go back now -- let's go back to President Tudjman's book, 1D00401. We've got the original language version that I'm told --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if possible, could Mr. Stringer leave this for after the break? With regard to Mr. Tudjman's theoretical ambushes, well, I wouldn't want to discuss this by having this text put before me - this is an academic work, I think I have the book - because this isn't serious. If possible. If not, I'll manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, what do you think of this? I assume that this is an important part of your case, this document, I mean. Would it be a problem for you to address this issue after the summer recess, or do you really want to put this question today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can come back to it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be useful if you got back to this. In the meantime, Mr. Praljak will have time to read the book, if he hasn't read it already, and he will therefore be able to answer your questions. And I think that is in everybody's interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll try, for the third time, to see if we can get the video to roll. And if it works, then we'll be able to continue with this part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, coming back, we spoke earlier about the conversation that Ed Vulliamy had with Mate Boban, where Boban explained his views on -- or his vision on Herceg-Bosna, if you will, and you voiced your agreement with much of what Boban said in that conversation. And I want to expand and I want to try to bring this down now and talk a little bit about your own views and your own vision for Herceg-Bosna because, as we know, you're originally from that area. And so I want to show you some of the things you said back in 1994, when these film clips were taken. So let's roll the first one, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Okay, I apologise, Mr. President. I don't think this is working, and I'm not going to waste any more time on this today. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since you granted my request, too, could we conclude with this? We have another 40 minutes. This is the fourth day -- the 40th day, and I can remain if necessary, but if not, it would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that you have had enough and you had rather we adjourn now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to make that request. I can continue, but as things aren't running smoothly, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, since we have technical problems and since Mr. Praljak is telling us that he had rather stop now because he is exhausted, I think it's for you to say. We have 40 minutes left, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This might be one of the few times that I agree with the general. I'm at the end of this binder, and if the videos aren't going to work, then I'm going to have to distribute the next binder before I can even continue. And so I think that given the fact that the video is not working, this is a logical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For two technical reasons, i.e., Mr. Tudjman's book, which Mr. Praljak would like to examine, and due to the fact that we cannot show the video and there's no soundtrack, and, third point, since the accused has asked for us to adjourn because he's tired and exhausted, we will adjourn for today, which means that we shall resume on Monday, the 17th of August. Mr. Stringer, you will then address the last binder with Mr. Tudjman's text, in addition to the video, and then we will move on to the next binders. Fine. The court stands adjourned, and we shall reconvene, as I have said, in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of August, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
